These exercises practise mixed-effects models with the lme4 package. lme4 is a large package, so **the first run on this page can take a minute** while your browser downloads it. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.


::: {.cell setup='true' exercise='["ex1","ex2","ex3","ex4","ex5"]'}
```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5]
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)
students  <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
panel <- semesters |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |>
  mutate(time = semester - 1)
```
:::


## Random intercepts and slopes

### Exercise 1: A first mixed model

Using `sleepstudy` (it comes with lme4), fit a random intercept model of reaction time on days, and calculate the ICC.


::: {.cell exercise='ex1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
model <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | ______), data = sleepstudy)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
vc$vcov[1] / sum(vc$vcov)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
model <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
vc$vcov[1] / sum(vc$vcov)
```

The ICC is about 0.59: most of the variation in reaction times is due to stable differences between people.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Does sleep change over the semesters?

Fit a random intercept model for `sleep_hours` over `time`. What is the ICC? Does sleep change? Use a confidence interval to decide.


::: {.cell exercise='ex2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
sleep_ri <- lmer(______ ~ time + (1 | student_id), data = panel)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(sleep_ri))
vc$vcov[1] / sum(vc$vcov)
confint(sleep_ri, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sleep_ri <- lmer(sleep_hours ~ time + (1 | student_id), data = panel)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(sleep_ri))
vc$vcov[1] / sum(vc$vcov)
confint(sleep_ri, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```

The ICC is about 0.83: students differ a lot in how much they sleep, but each student sleeps about the same from semester to semester. The confidence interval for `time` includes zero: sleep does not change over the two years.
:::
:::

### Exercise 3: Is a random slope worth it?

Add a random slope of `time` to the model from Exercise 2, and compare the two models with `anova()`.


::: {.cell exercise='ex3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
sleep_ri <- lmer(sleep_hours ~ time + (1 | student_id), data = panel)
sleep_rs <- lmer(sleep_hours ~ time + (______ | student_id), data = panel)
anova(sleep_ri, sleep_rs)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sleep_rs <- lmer(sleep_hours ~ time + (time | student_id), data = panel)
anova(sleep_ri, sleep_rs)
```

The random slope improves the model a little (p ≈ 0.02, and a slightly lower AIC), but the spread of the slopes is tiny (an SD of about 0.05 hours per semester; see `VarCorr(sleep_rs)`). Statistically worth keeping, practically unimportant: students' sleep is very stable.
:::
:::

## Interactions and levels

### Exercise 4: Do part-time students change differently?

Fit `wellbeing ~ time * study_mode + (time | student_id)`. Do part-time students start at a different level? Do they change at a different rate?


::: {.cell exercise='ex4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
wb_mode <- lmer(wellbeing ~ time * ______ + (time | student_id), data = panel)
round(summary(wb_mode)$coefficients, 2)
confint(wb_mode, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```
:::


::: { .hint exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`study_modePart-time` is the difference in level at time 0 (semester 1). `time:study_modePart-time` is the difference in slope. Check which confidence intervals include zero.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
wb_mode <- lmer(wellbeing ~ time * study_mode + (time | student_id), data = panel)
round(summary(wb_mode)$coefficients, 2)
confint(wb_mode, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```

Part-time students start almost 4 points lower (the interval excludes zero), but their wellbeing declines at the same rate as full-time students' (the interaction's interval includes zero). The gap is present from the start and stays about the same.
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: Do supervisors matter for study hours?

Fit a model for `study_hours` with random intercepts for supervisors and students, and calculate the share of variation at each level.


::: {.cell exercise='ex5'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
study_levels <- lmer(study_hours ~ time + (1 | ______) + (1 | student_id), data = panel)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(study_levels))
data.frame(level = vc$grp, share = round(vc$vcov / sum(vc$vcov), 3))
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
study_levels <- lmer(study_hours ~ time + (1 | supervisor_id) + (1 | student_id), data = panel)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(study_levels))
data.frame(level = vc$grp, share = round(vc$vcov / sum(vc$vcov), 3))
```

The supervisor share is zero, and R reports a singular fit: supervisors make no difference to how much students study. (They did matter for wellbeing.) Almost all the variation, about 91%, is between students.
:::
:::
